chapters.title: 3.1 Clicks, Typing, Clearing, Checkboxes/Radios, Selects
chapters.overviewText: Every Cypress action (.click, .type, .check, .select) runs an actionability checklist first: visible, non-zero size, not disabled, not animating, not covered. .type() always appends — it never replaces existing text — and {tab} is unsupported. .select() only works on native HTML <select> elements.
chapters.why: Actionability errors are the most common 'the element is right there' failures in Cypress. Interviewers distinguish engineers who diagnose coverage/disabled/hidden from those who reach for { force: true }. Knowing that .type() appends and that {tab} does not work prevents two first-week bugs that look like product defects.
chapters.when: Before writing any form or button interaction. Revisit whenever a click times out with 'covered by another element', a field keeps concatenating values, or Tab-based focus tests fail.

practical.scenario: Fill an already-populated employee search box, tick remote-work, pick a department from a native <select>, and submit while a loading overlay is fading out.
practical.pass: You .clear() before .type(), use .check() not .click() for the checkbox, .select('Quality Assurance') on the native select, and wait for the overlay to disappear instead of { force: true }.
practical.fail: You .type() into a pre-filled field (text concatenates), click a covered Submit with { force: true }, or try .type('{tab}') to move focus.

chapters.customSummary:
- Actionability: visible, not hidden, non-zero size, not disabled, not animating, not covered — Cypress retries then names the failed check.
- { force: true } skips the checklist — legitimate for by-design hidden inputs, not a default fix.
- .type() always appends; .clear() first to replace. Fires real keydown/keypress/keyup/input per character.
- {tab} is unsupported in .type(); {enter}, {backspace}, {selectall}, {esc}, modifiers work.
- .check()/.uncheck() are idempotent; radios use .check(value); .select() is native <select> only.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Actionability — what Cypress checks before it acts

Before `.click()`, `.type()`, `.clear()`, `.check()`, `.uncheck()`, or `.select()`, Cypress runs an actionability checklist on the subject. Conceptually parallel to Playwright's actionability checks, Cypress's specific criteria are:

- the element is not `display: none` / `visibility: hidden` / `opacity: 0`
- it has non-zero width and height
- it is not `disabled` (or `readonly` for typing)
- it is not currently animating
- it is not covered by another element (modal, spinner, sticky header)

If any check fails, Cypress retries until `defaultCommandTimeout` (4s by default), then fails with a diagnostic that names the check — e.g. "this element is being covered by another element". Hover the failed command in the Test Runner and inspect the restored DOM: you will usually see the covering overlay.

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=submit-leave]').click();
cy.get('[data-cy=leave-card]').dblclick();
cy.get('[data-cy=attachment-row]').rightclick();

cy.get('[data-cy=grid-cell]').click(40, 12); // x, y inside the element
cy.get('[data-cy=skill-chip]').click({ multiple: true });
```

`{ force: true }` skips **all** actionability checks and is available on essentially every action command, not just click. Legitimate use: a custom checkbox that visually hides the real `<input>` and styles a sibling — the real input is invisible *by design*. Illegitimate use: a loading spinner that never disappeared. Forcing the click papers over a product bug and a flaky test.

## `.type()` always appends

This is the first-week Cypress bug. Playwright's `.fill()` replaces the value; Cypress `.type()` **appends** to whatever is already in the field.

```js
// Wrong if the search box already contains last week's query:
cy.get('[data-cy=employee-search]').type('Simran Tamrakar');
// → "oldquerySimran Tamrakar"

// Right:
cy.get('[data-cy=employee-search]').clear().type('Simran Tamrakar');
cy.get('[data-cy=notes]').type('Hello{enter}World');
cy.get('[data-cy=search]').type('{selectall}{backspace}');
cy.get('[data-cy=search]').type('slow', { delay: 150 });
```

`.type()` fires real per-character keyboard events (`keydown`, `keypress`, `keyup`, `input`). There is no first-class "instant fill" the way Playwright splits `.fill()` vs `.type()`. The workaround for a huge string with no live keystroke listeners is `.invoke('val', longString).trigger('input')` so React/Vue still notice the change.

## `{tab}` is unsupported

Cypress special-character sequences include `{enter}`, `{backspace}`, `{del}`, `{esc}`, `{selectall}`, `{uparrow}` / `{downarrow}`, `{home}` / `{end}`, and modifiers (`{ctrl+a}`, `{shift+enter}`). **`{tab}` is not supported.** `.type('{tab}')` will not move focus. Cypress's documented position is that Tab-order is a browser concern you assert differently (focus the next field directly, or check `document.activeElement` after a real user-like click). If you truly need native Tab, `cypress-real-events` (`.realPress('Tab')`) is the community escape hatch — a plugin, not core.

## Checkboxes, radios, native selects

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=remote-checkbox]').check();
cy.get('[data-cy=newsletter]').uncheck();
cy.get('[data-cy=skills]').check(['Python', 'Cypress']); // by value
cy.get('[data-cy=employment-type]').check('full-time');  // radio by value

cy.get('[data-cy=department]').select('Quality Assurance'); // visible text
cy.get('[data-cy=department]').select('qa');                // value
cy.get('[data-cy=department]').select(2);                   // 0-based index
cy.get('[data-cy=skills-native]').select(['Python', 'Cypress']);
```

`.check()` / `.uncheck()` are **idempotent** — unlike `.click()`, which toggles. Radios in the same `name` group are mutually exclusive; there is no meaningful `.uncheck()` for a radio. `.select()` **only works on native `<select>`**. A styled `<div>` combobox from Ant Design, MUI, or React Select will fail `.select()` with "found no `<select>`". Custom dropdowns are the entire next chapter.

## vs Playwright

| | Cypress | Playwright |
|---|---|---|
| Replace field value | `.clear().type()` | `.fill()` |
| Event-accurate typing | `.type()` (the default) | `.type()` (opt-in vs fill) |
| Tab | unsupported in `.type()` | `page.keyboard.press('Tab')` |
| Actionability skip | `{ force: true }` | `force=True` |
| Native select | `.select()` | `select_option()` |

Interview-safe: "Cypress actions retry actionability until timeout and tell you *which* check failed. I do not default to `force`. I always `.clear()` before `.type()` because type appends. I never send `{tab}`. I only call `.select()` on a real `<select>.`"

chapters.title: 3.2 Forms & Inputs
chapters.overviewText: A form test is only as good as its post-submit assertion. Happy-path plus validation-failure is the minimum pair. Use 'have.value' for inputs (they have no child text), fire real events so controlled React/Vue fields update, and prefer submitting the way the user does — click or {enter} — not form.submit() unless you are deliberately skipping UI.
chapters.why: Shallow form tests ('the button was clickable') pass while onboarding, leave, and payroll forms silently drop fields. Interviewers look for the value-vs-text distinction, controlled-input event awareness, and a validation-error spec sitting next to the happy path.
chapters.when: Any create/edit form: onboarding, leave request, payroll run, profile. Revisit when a .type() 'succeeds' but the app submits empty because the framework never saw input events.

practical.scenario: Onboard Simran Tamrakar with department, start date, and remote flag; then prove required-field errors when submitting empty.
practical.pass: You type/select/check, click submit, assert a success banner *and* a separate spec that empty submit shows first-name and email errors. You use have.value on the email input.
practical.fail: You only assert the submit button is enabled, or you use contain/have.text on an <input> expecting the typed value.

chapters.customSummary:
- Assert the post-submit outcome (banner, row, URL), not merely that click did not throw.
- Every form needs a happy-path spec and a validation-failure spec.
- 'have.value' for input values; 'have.text'/'contain' for rendered text — <input> has no child text.
- .type()/.check()/.select() fire real events so controlled React/Vue state updates; .invoke('val') alone may not.
- Date/number/file inputs have extra constraints; native date often wants yyyy-mm-dd.

chapters.title: 3.3 Dropdowns
chapters.overviewText: Native <select> uses .select(text|value|index). Everything else — React Select, Ant Design Select, MUI Autocomplete, custom comboboxes — is a three-step interaction: open the trigger, wait for the options list, click the option. Options often render in a React portal on document.body, so querying inside the trigger's .within() finds nothing.
chapters.why: Modern HRM dashboards almost never ship a raw <select> for department, leave type, or approver. Treating custom dropdowns as .select() is a frequent interview trip. The portal caveat explains a class of 'I can see the option in the screenshot but cy.get cannot' bugs.
chapters.when: Any styled dropdown, searchable combobox, or multi-select. Revisit when options exist in the DOM but .within() on the field wrapper cannot see them.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — leave type and approver pickers (Ant Design / React Select)
practical.scenario: Choose 'Annual Leave' from a custom combobox whose list renders in a portal, then a native country <select> on a tax form.
practical.pass: You click the combobox, then cy.contains('.ant-select-item', 'Annual Leave').click() on the body-level list; you .select() only the native country field. You do not wrap the option click in .within() of the closed field.
practical.fail: You call .select('Annual Leave') on a div combobox, or you .within() the trigger and look for options that live under document.body.

chapters.customSummary:
- .select() is native <select> only — by text, value, or index; array for multiple.
- Custom dropdown 3-step: (1) click trigger (2) wait for list to exist (3) click the option.
- Portal caveat: option lists often mount on document.body — .within() on the field misses them.
- Searchable comboboxes: type into the input, then click the filtered option — do not assume .select().
- Assert the selected display value after close, not only that an option was clicked.

chapters.title: 3.4 Hover, Drag-and-Drop, Scrolling
chapters.overviewText: Cypress has no .hover() command. CSS :hover is not reliably triggered by .trigger('mouseover'). Drag-and-drop is not one API: HTML5 drag uses dataTransfer events, mouse-based DnD uses mousedown/mousemove/mouseup, and libraries like dnd-kit often need cypress-real-events or a dedicated plugin. Scrolling is usually automatic for actionability; cy.scrollTo and .scrollIntoView cover the rest.
chapters.why: Interviewers use hover and drag as architecture questions: Cypress runs in-page JS and cannot synthesize OS-level mouse the way Playwright's CDP can. Knowing the mechanisms — and when to reach for cypress-real-events — is the senior answer, not 'Cypress cannot hover.'
chapters.when: Tooltip/popover menus, kanban leave-approval boards, infinite payroll tables, sticky headers covering a button. Revisit when :hover CSS never appears in snapshots.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — leave kanban plus overflow table
practical.scenario: Reveal a tooltip on the leave-balance badge, drag a request card from Pending to Approved, then click a Submit that sits below the fold under a sticky header.
practical.pass: You use .trigger('mouseover') or .realHover() for the tooltip; you pick an HTML5 or mouse-event drag mechanism (or a plugin) that matches the board library; you .scrollIntoView() or rely on actionability rather than a fixed cy.wait.
practical.fail: You write cy.get(el).hover(), or a single .trigger('drop') with no dataTransfer on an HTML5 board, or you { force: true } the covered Submit.

chapters.customSummary:
- There is no cy.hover() / .hover() in core Cypress.
- .trigger('mouseover'|'mouseenter') fires JS events but often does not apply CSS :hover; cypress-real-events .realHover() is the usual workaround.
- Drag mechanisms: HTML5 dataTransfer events, mouse down/move/up, @4tw/cypress-drag-drop, cypress-real-events — match the app's library.
- Actionability auto-scrolls the subject into view; cy.scrollTo / .scrollIntoView for windows and nested overflow panes.

chapters.title: 3.5 Tables, Lists & Dynamic Content
chapters.overviewText: The Cypress row-finding idiom is cy.contains(rowSelector, text).find(actionSelector) — contains scoped to the row yields the <tr> (or list item), then find() acts inside it. cy.get('tr').contains(text) yields the cell instead, so a following .click() hits the wrong element. Dynamic lists belong behind intercept aliases, not fixed waits.
chapters.why: HRM UIs are tables: leave queues, employee directories, payroll registers. Wrong yield (cell vs row) is the classic 'clicked the name, not Approve'. Interviewers listen for the contains(selector, text) idiom by name.
chapters.when: Any grid, queue, or virtualized list. Revisit when a test clicks the first row's button instead of the matching employee's, or when rows appear after a fetch.

practical.scenario: Approve Simran Tamrakar's Annual Leave row among many pending requests that load from GET /api/leave-requests.
practical.pass: You cy.wait('@leaveList'), then cy.contains('tr', 'Simran Tamrakar').find('[data-cy=approve]').click(), then assert that row shows Approved.
practical.fail: You cy.get('tr').eq(0) or cy.get('tr').contains('Simran').click() (clicks the cell), or you cy.wait(2000) for the table to fill.

chapters.customSummary:
- Idiom: cy.contains('tr', 'Simran Tamrakar').find('[data-cy=approve]') — contains(selector, text) yields the row.
- cy.get('tr').contains(text) yields the matching cell, not the row — chaining .find()/.click() then acts on the wrong node.
- Filter, sort, pagination: assert row count and a named cell, not visual position alone.
- Dynamic/virtualized lists: intercept + wait, then query; do not eq(n) on a still-loading tbody.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The row-finding idiom

```js
cy.contains('tr', 'Simran Tamrakar')
  .find('[data-cy=approve]')
  .click();

cy.contains('tr', 'Simran Tamrakar')
  .should('contain', 'Approved');
```

`cy.contains(selector, text)` means: find an element matching `selector` that contains this text (possibly in a descendant). The **yielded subject is the `tr`**, so `.find()` looks at cells inside that row. This is the Cypress-idiomatic way to "act on the row for employee X".

The version people write first is wrong in a subtle way:

```js
// Yields the <td> that contains the name, not the <tr>
cy.get('tr').contains('Simran Tamrakar').click();
```

`.click()` then hits the name cell. `.find('[data-cy=approve]')` off that cell finds nothing (the button is a sibling cell). `cy.get('tbody tr').eq(0)` is worse: it couples the test to sort order.

Works the same for lists:

```js
cy.contains('[data-cy=employee-card]', 'Simran Tamrakar')
  .find('[data-cy=view-profile]')
  .click();
```

## Tables: headers, counts, empty states

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=leave-table] thead').should('contain', 'Employee');
cy.get('[data-cy=leave-table] tbody tr').should('have.length', 3);
cy.contains('No pending requests').should('be.visible');
```

Assert a named cell, not "the third column of the second row," unless you are specifically testing column order. For computed payroll amounts, `cy.contains('tr', 'Simran').find('[data-cy=net-pay]').should('contain', '85,000')`.

## Dynamic content

Rows that appear after `GET /api/leave-requests` need a wait strategy from 3.11:

```js
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/leave-requests').as('leaveList');
cy.visit('/leave/approvals');
cy.wait('@leaveList');
cy.contains('tr', 'Simran Tamrakar').should('be.visible');
```

Alternatively, skip the alias and let `.should('have.length', 3)` retry until the tbody fills — fine when you only care about UI. Use the alias when you must assert payload or when the empty state and the loaded table are easy to confuse.

**Virtualized tables** (react-window) unmount off-screen rows. `cy.contains('tr', 'Name at row 500')` will not find a DOM node that was recycled. Scroll the container (3.4) until the row mounts, or assert via search/filter instead of raw scroll-to-index unless virtualization itself is under test.

**Live updates** (new leave request appears without reload): intercept the poll/websocket-adjacent fetch, or assert with a long-retrying `cy.contains` after the triggering action. Do not `cy.wait(5000)`.

## vs Playwright

Playwright `get_by_role('row', { name: 'Simran Tamrakar' }).get_by_role('button', { name: 'Approve' })` is the accessibility-shaped version of the same idea. Cypress's `contains(sel, text).find()` is the jQuery-shaped version. Both beat nth-child.

chapters.title: 3.6 Handling iframes
chapters.overviewText: cy.get() cannot see into an iframe's document by default — Cypress commands run against the AUT's top document. Same-origin iframes use the contentDocument.body wrap pattern (or cypress-iframe). Cross-origin iframes (Stripe, Okta widgets) hit the same-origin policy; cy.origin() may help a full-page navigation, not a foreign iframe you do not control.
chapters.why: Payment and e-signature widgets are iframes. Playwright's frame_locator is first-class; Cypress requires a documented recipe. Knowing the same-origin pattern vs 'this iframe is untestable in Cypress' is the honest architecture answer from Part 0.
chapters.when: Embedded HTML editors, same-origin preview panes, third-party payment/signature widgets. Revisit when cy.get('[data-cy=card-number]') times out and the field is visibly inside an iframe in DevTools.

practical.app: Bizlevate TADA / payroll — same-origin policy iframe vs Stripe card widget
practical.scenario: Fill a same-origin policy-acknowledgement iframe, then decide how far to test a Stripe Elements card iframe.
practical.pass: You use the contentDocument.body + cy.wrap pattern (or cypress-iframe) for same-origin. For Stripe you treat the widget as out of scope or use Stripe test APIs — you do not expect cy.get to pierce cross-origin.
practical.fail: You cy.get the card number in the parent document, or you assume cy.origin() magically enters a nested third-party iframe.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cypress does not query iframe documents by default — more ceremony than Playwright frame_locator().
- Same-origin pattern: cy.get('iframe').its('0.contentDocument.body').should('not.be.empty').then(cy.wrap).find(...).
- cypress-iframe: cy.frameLoaded() + cy.iframe() is a plugin convenience over the same idea.
- Cross-origin iframes are blocked by the browser; Cypress cannot honestly E2E a Stripe inner form.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why `cy.get` misses iframe contents

An iframe is a nested browsing context with its own `document`. Cypress commands target the application's document (the AUT inside Cypress's runner iframe). They do not automatically recurse into child frames. Playwright's external driver enumerates frames as first-class objects (`frame_locator`); Cypress's in-page model starts more restrictive even for **same-origin** frames.

Open DevTools on a failing test: if the input lives under `#payment-iframe` → `#document` → `input`, your parent-document selector will never retry successfully.

## Same-origin pattern (core Cypress)

Official recipe — no plugin required when the iframe `src` is same-origin (or `srcdoc`):

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=policy-iframe]')
  .its('0.contentDocument.body')
  .should('not.be.empty')
  .then(cy.wrap)
  .find('[data-cy=acknowledge]')
  .check();

cy.get('[data-cy=policy-iframe]')
  .its('0.contentDocument.body')
  .then(cy.wrap)
  .find('[data-cy=policy-accept]')
  .click();
```

Walkthrough: `.its('0.contentDocument.body')` reaches the iframe's DOM (jQuery collection index 0). `.should('not.be.empty')` retries until the inner document has loaded. `cy.wrap` turns the raw body back into a Cypress subject so `.find()` is a Cypress command with retry-ability.

If you skip `should('not.be.empty')`, you race the iframe load. If you skip `cy.wrap`, you cannot chain Cypress commands on a naked DOM node.

## `cypress-iframe` plugin

```js
// npm i -D cypress-iframe
// support/e2e.js: import 'cypress-iframe';

cy.frameLoaded('[data-cy=policy-iframe]');
cy.iframe('[data-cy=policy-iframe]')
  .find('[data-cy=acknowledge]')
  .check();
```

This is sugar over the same `contentDocument` access. Use it if the team wants readable specs; know the core pattern for interviews and for environments that ban extra plugins.

## Cross-origin iframes

The browser's same-origin policy blocks reading `contentDocument` of `https://js.stripe.com` from your app origin. Cypress cannot patch around that any more than your app's own JavaScript can. `cy.origin()` re-injects test code for a **top-level** navigation to another origin (Part 9.1). It is not a general "enter this nested Stripe iframe" API.

Practical options for a Stripe/PayPal widget:

- Do not E2E the inner PAN field; assert your app opened the widget and complete payment via test tokens / API stubs (Part 5).
- If the third party offers a same-origin test harness, use that in a dedicated spec.
- If the suite *must* drive the inner iframe, that is a concrete Playwright reason (Part 0.4).

## Nested iframes and multiple frames

Chain `.its('0.contentDocument.body').then(cy.wrap).find('iframe')` again for same-origin nesting. Prefer `data-cy` on the outer iframe element so you do not grab the wrong frame when the page has several.

## vs Playwright

```js
// Playwright (conceptual): page.frame_locator('#policy').get_by_label('I agree')
```

Same test, less ceremony, including many cross-origin cases. Cypress: same-origin recipe or plugin; cross-origin nested widgets are an architecture stop sign, not a missing import.

chapters.title: 3.7 File Uploads
chapters.overviewText: .selectFile() is a core Cypress command since 9.3 — you do not need cypress-file-upload for new work. Pass a fixture path, an array of files, or an in-memory contents object. { action: 'drag-drop' } fires drop events for drop-zone UIs; the default action sets the hidden <input type=file>.
chapters.why: Older Stack Overflow answers still prescribe cypress-file-upload's .attachFile(). Interviewers notice whether you know the built-in command and the version floor. Drop-zones that only listen for drop will ignore a default selectFile.
chapters.when: Resume upload, expense receipts, bulk employee CSV import. Revisit when a drop-zone ignores the file or when a tutorial tells you to install cypress-file-upload on Cypress 13.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — onboarding resume + TADA receipt drop-zone
practical.scenario: Attach resume.pdf via a hidden file input, then drop a receipt PNG onto a drag-and-drop zone.
practical.pass: You .selectFile('cypress/fixtures/resume.pdf') on the input and .selectFile(..., { action: 'drag-drop' }) on the zone. You assert the filename chip / upload success, not only that the command queued.
practical.fail: You add cypress-file-upload on a 9.3+ project as if it were required, or you default-selectFile a drop-zone that only handles drop events.

chapters.customSummary:
- .selectFile() is built-in since Cypress 9.3; cypress-file-upload is legacy.
- Paths are relative to the project root (typically cypress/fixtures/...).
- { action: 'drag-drop' } for drop zones; default action for <input type=file>.
- contents + fileName + mimeType for in-memory files without a fixture on disk.
- Assert the UI result (chip, preview, POST via intercept) after the select.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## `.selectFile()` since 9.3

For years Cypress had no upload command; `cypress-file-upload` (`.attachFile()`) was universal. **Cypress 9.3 added `.selectFile()` to core.** New tests should use the built-in. Recognize `.attachFile` in old code; do not add the plugin on a modern Cypress just because a blog post says so.

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=resume-upload]').selectFile('cypress/fixtures/resume.pdf');

cy.get('[data-cy=attachments]').selectFile([
  'cypress/fixtures/id-front.png',
  'cypress/fixtures/id-back.png',
]);
```

Paths are from the project root (where `cypress.config` lives), not from the spec file.

## Drop-zones vs file inputs

Default action: set files on an `<input type="file">` (including `display:none` inputs — this is a legitimate `{ force: true }` / hidden-input case; `.selectFile` can target the input directly).

If the UI is a big "drop files here" surface whose JS listens for `drop` and **does not** wire a hidden input, the default action never runs the app code:

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=receipt-dropzone]').selectFile(
  'cypress/fixtures/taxi-receipt.png',
  { action: 'drag-drop' },
);
```

`action: 'select'` (default) vs `'drag-drop'` is the difference between setting `input.files` and dispatching drag events. Match the widget.

## In-memory files

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=csv-import]').selectFile({
  contents: Cypress.Buffer.from('employeeId,name\n1,Simran Tamrakar\n'),
  fileName: 'employees.csv',
  mimeType: 'text/csv',
});
```

Useful when you do not want a fixture on disk, or when the file must include today's date. `Cypress.Buffer` is the bundled buffer helper.

## What to assert

Selecting a file is not a complete test. Assert the filename chip, a preview thumbnail, disabled Submit until upload finishes, or:

```js
cy.intercept('POST', '/api/employees/*/resume').as('resumeUpload');
cy.get('[data-cy=resume-upload]').selectFile('cypress/fixtures/resume.pdf');
cy.wait('@resumeUpload').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 201);
```

## vs Playwright

Playwright `locator.set_input_files()` is the analogue. Cypress's `{ action: 'drag-drop' }` is the extra knob for drop-zones. Both should use fixtures, not production PII files.

chapters.title: 3.8 File Downloads & Verification
chapters.overviewText: Cypress has no expect_download() API. The browser writes files to downloadsFolder (cypress/downloads/ by default). Poll with cy.readFile({ timeout }) for text/CSV; use cy.task to parse XLSX/PDF in Node. You are verifying a file on disk, not a download event.
chapters.why: Payslip PDFs and payroll CSVs are core HRM artifacts. Playwright waits on a download event; Cypress checks the folder. Knowing downloadsFolder + retrying readFile + task-based binary parse is the complete Cypress answer.
chapters.when: Export payroll, download payslip, CSV dump of the employee directory. Revisit when readFile flakes (file not finished) or when you need to assert Excel sheets.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — payroll CSV export and payslip PDF
practical.scenario: Click Export, then prove the CSV contains Employee ID and Simran's row; optionally parse a PDF payslip.
practical.pass: You click export, cy.readFile the path under Cypress.config('downloadsFolder') with a timeout, assert contents, and cy.task a parser for XLSX/PDF. You do not look for a Playwright-style download event.
practical.fail: You only assert the button click, or you cy.readFile immediately with no timeout while the file is still writing, or you try to parse XLSX in the browser with cy.readFile alone.

chapters.customSummary:
- No first-class download event; files land in downloadsFolder (default cypress/downloads/).
- cy.readFile(path, { timeout }) retries until the file exists — that is the wait.
- Text/CSV: assert with should('contain') / parse in .then().
- XLSX/PDF: cy.task in setupNodeEvents (SheetJS, pdf-parse) — Node, not the browser.
- Prefer cy.request the export URL when you only need bytes, not the click-to-download chrome.

chapters.title: 3.9 Handling alert, confirm, prompt
chapters.overviewText: Cypress auto-accepts window.alert and window.confirm — the opposite of Playwright, which fails if a dialog is unhandled. Override with cy.on('window:confirm') and return false to simulate Cancel. There is no prompt event; stub window.prompt so it returns a string.
chapters.why: Delete-employee and cancel-payroll flows use confirm(). If you only ever exercise the auto-OK path, the Cancel path is untested. Stubbing prompt is a Sinon skill that also appears in 3.13. Never confuse native dialogs with in-app modal divs.
chapters.when: Native window.alert/confirm/prompt only. Styled 'Are you sure?' modals are ordinary DOM (3.1). Revisit when a test hangs on Playwright muscle-memory or when Cancel never runs.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — delete employee (confirm) and rename department (prompt)
practical.scenario: Delete with default OK, delete with Cancel, and rename via prompt returning 'People Ops'.
practical.pass: You rely on auto-accept for OK; cy.on('window:confirm', () => false) for Cancel; cy.stub(win, 'prompt').returns('People Ops') before the click. You assert the dialog message text.
practical.fail: You look for a Cypress .alert() command, or you cy.get the native dialog as if it were DOM, or you leave prompt unstubbed and hope.

chapters.customSummary:
- alert() and confirm() are auto-accepted; the message is logged — opposite of Playwright's fail-if-unhandled default.
- cy.on('window:alert'|'window:confirm', handler) to assert text; return false from confirm to click Cancel.
- prompt() has no dedicated event — cy.stub(win, 'prompt').returns('...').
- In-app modal dialogs are not window.confirm — use normal clicks.

chapters.title: 3.10 Cookies & Local/Session Storage
chapters.overviewText: cy.setCookie / getCookie / clearCookies are core commands. localStorage and sessionStorage are usually read via cy.window() (cy.clearLocalStorage is core; Cypress 12 added clearAllLocalStorage / clearAllSessionStorage). testIsolation: true (the Cypress 12+ default) clears cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage between tests — do not expect leftovers unless you turned isolation off.
chapters.why: Auth tokens live in cookies or storage. Tests that 'mysteriously' log out are often testIsolation doing its job. Tests that 'mysteriously' stay logged in are isolation disabled or cy.session. Part 7 goes deeper; this chapter is the raw API you must not get wrong.
chapters.when: Seeding a session cookie, asserting a theme key, debugging empty storage at test start. Revisit Part 7 when you need cy.session() instead of copy-pasting setCookie.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — JWT cookie plus theme in localStorage
practical.scenario: Set a session cookie, assert dark theme from localStorage, then explain why the next test starts logged out.
practical.pass: You use cy.setCookie/getCookie, window.localStorage.setItem/getItem (or clearLocalStorage), and you name testIsolation as the reason storage is empty in the following test.
practical.fail: You assume localStorage survives to the next it(), or you call a non-existent cy.setLocalStorage as if it were core Cypress.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cookies: cy.setCookie, getCookie, getCookies, clearCookie, clearCookies; Cypress 12+ also clearAllCookies.
- Storage writes: cy.window().then(win => win.localStorage / sessionStorage). cy.clearLocalStorage is core; set/get helpers are plugins, not core.
- testIsolation (default true since Cypress 12) clears cookies + localStorage + sessionStorage between tests.
- cy.session() (Part 7) caches and restores this state — these commands are its building blocks.

chapters.title: 3.11 Waiting Strategies
chapters.overviewText: Wait hierarchy: (1) retrying commands and .should() (2) cy.wait('@alias') after cy.intercept (3) per-command timeout (4) cy.wait(ms) last, with a comment. cy.wait(3000) and cy.wait('@getUsers') share a name and mean opposite things. Timeouts: defaultCommandTimeout, requestTimeout, responseTimeout, pageLoadTimeout.
chapters.why: Numeric waits are the leading cause of Cypress flakes and slow suites. Interviewers want the hierarchy recited in order — not 'I always intercept' and not 'I always wait 2 seconds.'
chapters.when: Any test that feels racy: tables populating, buttons enabling, navigations. Revisit when someone pastes cy.wait(5000) as a 'fix.'

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — dashboard widgets + leave submit
practical.scenario: Visit dashboard (GET /api/dashboard), submit leave (POST), then see the success toast.
practical.pass: You intercept+wait the dashboard GET if you care about the network; you let .should('be.visible') retry the toast; you never lead with cy.wait(3000).
practical.fail: You cy.wait(3000) after every click, or you confuse cy.wait('@alias') with a sleep, or you wrap a DOM expect inside .then() and lose retries.

chapters.customSummary:
- Hierarchy: retrying .should() → cy.wait('@alias') → longer command timeout → cy.wait(ms) last resort.
- cy.wait(ms) is a sleep; cy.wait('@alias') waits for a named intercept — same command, different argument.
- Timeouts: defaultCommandTimeout (commands), requestTimeout/responseTimeout (network), pageLoadTimeout (visit).
- .should() retries the preceding query; expect() inside .then() does not.

chapters.title: 3.12 Mocking Dates & Timers
chapters.overviewText: cy.clock() replaces Date, setTimeout, setInterval, and (optionally) requestAnimationFrame in the AUT. Install the clock BEFORE cy.visit() so the app's first Date.now() is already frozen. cy.tick(ms) advances fake time without waiting on the wall clock — leave-balance year boundaries and toast dismissals become deterministic.
chapters.why: Leave accrues on calendar year; toasts die after 5s; 'overdue' badges use Date. Sleeping 5s is how suites get slow and flaky. Interviewers listen for 'clock before visit' — clock after visit misses constructors that already ran.
chapters.when: Anything that reads today's date or schedules a timer. Revisit when toasts, countdowns, or fiscal-year logic flake around midnight or in CI timezones.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — leave year remaining + auto-dismiss toast
practical.scenario: Freeze date at 2026-12-31, assert '0 days remaining this year', submit leave, tick 5s, assert toast gone — without a real 5s wait.
practical.pass: You cy.clock(Date.UTC(2026, 11, 31)) then cy.visit, interact, cy.tick(5000), assert. You restore with cy.clock().invoke('restore') only if needed.
practical.fail: You cy.visit then cy.clock (app already read Date), or you cy.wait(5000) for the toast, or you freeze Date and break an analytics SDK without narrowing the stubbed methods.

chapters.customSummary:
- cy.clock() before cy.visit() (or in onBeforeLoad) so the app boots under fake time.
- cy.tick(ms) advances timers and Date together without wall-clock wait.
- Default stubs: setTimeout, setInterval, Date; pass a method list if stubbing Date breaks a third party.
- cy.clock(now) sets the starting epoch; month in Date.UTC is 0-based.

chapters.title: 3.13 Spies & Stubs
chapters.overviewText: cy.spy wraps a function and records calls but still runs the original. cy.stub replaces the function (unless callsThrough). cy.intercept spies or stubs network (fetch/XHR), not arbitrary functions. All three are Sinon under the hood; Sinon-Chai gives called / calledWith. Pick the layer: function vs HTTP.
chapters.why: Interviewers ask 'spy vs stub vs mock vs intercept' to see if you know the layer. Stubbing window.open, spying console.error, and intercepting POST /api/leave are three different tools. Using intercept to 'spy' a method — or stub to fake an API — is the mix-up.
chapters.when: window.print, window.open, analytics.track, Date (prefer cy.clock), prompt (3.9), console.error. Network belongs to intercept (Part 5) even though the vocabulary overlaps "stub the endpoint."

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — payslip print + leave submit + analytics
practical.scenario: Click Print without a dialog, prove analytics.track('leave_submitted') fired with leaveType Annual, and still let GET /api/leave-requests hit the real server while recording it.
practical.pass: You stub window.print, spy analytics.track (or stub if you must not send), intercept GET without a fixture to spy the network. You assert calledOnce / calledWith.
practical.fail: You use cy.intercept to fake window.print, or cy.stub to fake an HTTP response, or you wrap a spy after the app already captured the original function reference.

chapters.customSummary:
- spy: wrap + record + call through. stub: replace + record (optionally returns/throws).
- intercept: HTTP fetch/XHR only — spy (no fixture) or stub (fixture/status).
- Install spies/stubs before the code path runs (onBeforeLoad / before click).
- Sinon-Chai: should('have.been.calledOnce'), calledWith — aliases via .as('print').

chapters.title: 3.14 Event Handling — Cypress.on() / cy.on()
chapters.overviewText: Cypress.on() binds Cypress-lifecycle events and is not auto-removed — put it in support files or always Cypress.off. cy.on() binds to the current AUT window and unbinds when the test ends. uncaught:exception can return false to swallow an error; never return false unconditionally or you will hide real product bugs.
chapters.why: A blanket Cypress.on('uncaught:exception', () => false) in support/e2e.js is one of the most damaging Cypress snippets on the internet. Interviewers treat it as a red flag. Knowing Cypress.on vs cy.on lifetime is how you avoid leaking a confirm handler into the next test.
chapters.when: Native dialogs (3.9), third-party ResizeObserver noise, fail hooks, window:before:load. Revisit whenever a support-file event handler makes later tests mysteriously pass or skip failures.

practical.app: Bizlevate HRM — SPA with ResizeObserver noise + delete confirm
practical.scenario: Stop ResizeObserver loop errors from failing tests without swallowing TypeErrors from leave submit, and bind confirm Cancel only in one spec.
practical.pass: You allowlist ResizeObserver in Cypress.on('uncaught:exception') by message; you cy.on('window:confirm') in the test. You never return false for all exceptions.
practical.fail: You Cypress.on('uncaught:exception', () => false) in support, or you Cypress.on('window:confirm') in a test and leak Cancel into the rest of the suite.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cypress.on: Cypress-level, persists until Cypress.off — use in support for process-wide handlers.
- cy.on: AUT/window, test-scoped — dialogs, unload, before:load for one test.
- uncaught:exception: return false only for a known allowlist; never blanket false.
- Other events: fail, window:alert, window:confirm, window:before:load, uncaught:exception.
